lines: Night of May 18, 1951,
Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province. Mount Yongmun.
At the headquarters of the Chinese 63rd Army... there was no doubt.
s02.label: Dramatization

lines: "The enemy ahead is the same division we shattered a month ago."
s03.label: Dramatization
bubbles:
We broke them
a month ago!

lines: They were not wrong.
Just one month earlier, at Sachang-ri... the ROK 6th Division had collapsed under a Chinese assault.
It abandoned its equipment, fled over the mountains, and scattered.
s05.label: Troops on a mountain road (Feb 1951)

lines: So the Chinese committed three divisions at once.
Three divisions, against one.
On paper... it was a battle that would be over in a single night.
s07.big: A Battle Decided in One Night?

lines: Yet ten days later,
it was the Chinese who were on the run.
s08.text:
Ten days later,
they stood at the edge of a lake

lines: And at the end of that road... a vast lake was waiting.
s09.label: Hwacheon Dam & Reservoir (1951)

lines: This is the story of how a defeated army rose again.
And how one lake came to be called... 'The Lake That Defeated the Invaders.'
s10.title: Battle of Yongmunsan & Lake Paro

lines: Spring, 1951.
The Chinese launched what became known as the Spring Offensive.
The first phase came in April. The second, in mid-May.
The objective was clear.
Drive the United Nations forces off the peninsula.
At the very least, retake Seoul.
The ROK 6th Division was attached to the U.S. Ninth Corps.
Its sector: north of Yangpyeong, around Mount Yongmun.
A rugged peak rising eleven hundred and fifty-seven meters.
s15.label: Rugged terrain of the central front (1951)

lines: The division commander was Brigadier General Chang Do-yong.
He used this terrain to set up an unusual deployment.
s16.name: Chang Do-yong

lines: Forward, he placed a single unit, the 2nd Regiment, as an outpost.
Behind it, on the main line of resistance, the 7th and 19th Regiments.
A forward outpost exists to warn of the enemy's approach and to buy time.
It is not meant to fight a decisive battle.
On the other side stood the Chinese 63rd Army.
The 187th, 188th, and 189th Divisions.
Their plan was simple.
Infiltrate by night, encircle, and break the line.
Just as they had done at Sachang-ri.
But the Chinese did not know one thing.
What the men of the 6th Division had sworn to themselves in that month.
s21.label: Dramatization

lines: The night of May 18th.
The Chinese attack began.
s22.label: Night flares (1951)

lines: Bugles sounded in the darkness...
and hundreds, then thousands, climbed the ridgelines.
s23.label: Dramatization

lines: They ran straight into the 2nd Regiment.
The forward outpost.
And here came the first reversal.
The 2nd Regiment did not fall back.
s26.label: Dramatization

lines: Under wave after wave of attacks, the 2nd Regiment was quickly encircled on three sides.
With communications barely holding, Colonel Song Dae-hoo and his men refused to yield, and fought to the last.
sA2.label: Dramatization

lines: In response, U.S. Ninth Corps artillery and supporting units laid down an unprecedented barrage, right in front of the friendly positions,
and the northern ridges of Mount Yongmun were pounded through the night.
sA4.label: U.S. 203mm howitzer (Korean War)

lines: This was a unit expected to hold briefly, then withdraw.
But the 2nd Regiment held its ground.
Surrounded, running low on ammunition... it held.
s27.label: Hill fighting (Korean War)

lines: And so the Chinese command made a fatal misjudgment.
"They're holding this hard... this must be the main line."
s28.label: Dramatization

lines: The Chinese kept pouring three divisions into this one small position.
May 19th, and on into the 20th.
Each night they surged in like waves. Each dawn they fell back, leaving only their dead.
s30.label: Infantry advancing on a hill (1951)

lines: The 6th Division's records report the slopes in front of the position covered with Chinese dead.
s31.head: AFTER-ACTION REPORT
rows: PLACE   : 2nd Regt position, N. of Mt. Yongmun
SUMMARY : Numerous enemy dead on forward slopes

lines: And behind that position... American artillery fired without pause.
s32.label: 155mm howitzer firing (Korean War)

lines: Three days.
For the three days the 2nd Regiment held, the Chinese were wearing down.
Out of rations, out of ammunition... and out of time.
Then came May 21st.
The 6th Division was ordered to counterattack.
The 7th and 19th Regiments, waiting on the main line,
moved forward together.
In that moment, the attacker became the hunted.
s36.label: Dramatization

lines: The exhausted Chinese began to break.
The retreat soon became a rout...
and the 6th Division gave chase without stopping.
s37.label: UN troops on the march (Korean War)

lines: Past Gapyeong, along the Bukhan River, northward.
And at the end of that road... the Hwacheon Reservoir.
Cut off, the Chinese forces were driven to the water's edge.
Deep water ahead. ROK and UN forces closing from behind.
Many fell here, drowned, or were taken prisoner.
s40.label: Chinese POWs captured by ROK forces

lines: Pushing north to retake the Hwacheon power plant and dam, the ROK 6th Division pressed in from all sides on the Chinese troops trapped around the reservoir.
Blocked by rugged mountains and cold water, the retreating enemy's command structure collapsed entirely,
and the Hwacheon area became the final graveyard of the Chinese Spring Offensive.
sB2.label: Captured Chinese soldiers (Korean War)
callouts: The Graveyard of the Spring Offensive

lines: Years later, President Syngman Rhee gave this lake a new name.
Lake Paro.
s41.name: Syngman Rhee

lines: Pa, to destroy. Ro, the invaders. Ho, the lake.
The division defeated just a month earlier... had renamed a lake.
s43.label: Hwacheon Reservoir (July 1951)
callouts: Lake Paro: "The Lake That Defeated the Invaders"

lines: So how did one division hold off three?
Let's break it down into four factors.
First, the deception of the forward outpost.
s45.title: Forward Outpost Deception

lines: Because the 2nd Regiment held far longer than expected, the Chinese misjudged the main axis of the defense.
With their forces massed in one place, the two regiments behind it prepared a counterattack almost untouched.
Intended or not... this was the first move that decided the battle.
s47.label: ROK 1st Division soldiers (1951)

lines: Second, firepower.
s48.title: Asymmetric Firepower

lines: The Chinese relied on mass, the so-called human wave.
Behind the 6th Division stood American artillery and air support.
And the denser the waves climbing the slopes... the heavier the toll the shells would take.
s50.label: Artillery fire (Korean War)

lines: Third, supply.
s51.title: Logistical Collapse

lines: Chinese soldiers fought with the food and ammunition they carried on their backs.
That was enough for roughly one week.
s52.label: Dramatization
bubbles:
This is all
the food left...

lines: UN forces called it 'the one-week offensive.'
By the time the 2nd Regiment had held for three days... the Chinese clock had all but run out.
s53.title: 'The One-Week Offensive'

lines: Fourth, terrain and morale.
Rising above eleven hundred meters, Mount Yongmun favored the defender.
And above all... the 6th Division carried the scar of Sachang-ri.
The memory of that defeat, and the vow never to retreat again, held the line.
s55.label: ROK soldiers (Korean War)

lines: Official South Korean histories credit this series of battles with more than seventeen thousand Chinese killed and over two thousand captured.
The 6th Division's own losses... numbered in the hundreds.
s56.note: Per official South Korean war history

lines: Of course, wartime figures are prone to exaggeration.
Claims that 'tens of thousands drowned' at Lake Paro are treated with caution by historians.
But one fact is clear.
After this battle, the Chinese Spring Offensive... could go no further.
Today, Lake Paro is quiet.
Fishing boats drift, and mist rises off the water.
s59.label: Lake Paro today (illustration)

lines: But beneath that water...
lie the lost years of countless young men who never came home.
The men of the 2nd Regiment who held the ridges of Mount Yongmun.
Most of them were around twenty years old.
Ordinary young men who had left their parents at home.
s61.label: Young men heading to the front (1950)

lines: And the Chinese soldiers who fell by the lake...
were, for the most part, young men too, sent to a foreign land.
s62.label: Prisoners of war (Korean War)

lines: The lesson of Yongmunsan is simple.
A single defeat does not decide the fate of an army.
And in war, the real weapon... is not numbers alone.
quotes: One defeat does not decide an army's fate
The real weapon is not numbers alone

lines: In one month, from a defeated division to a victorious one.
And in between... were the men who decided to stand again.
s64.label: The central front, 1951

We'll continue to bring the forgotten records of war to light.
s65.title:
May 1951. Mount Yongmun.
And Lake Paro.
